title: What made the donkey and the elephant political?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how the donkey and elephant became symbols of the American Democratic and Republican parties, centered on 19th-century political cartoonist Thomas Nast. They cover Nast's background and woodcut work, his popularization of Uncle Sam and the modern Santa Claus, and his Harper's Weekly years. They trace the donkey's first appearance in 1870 (the Copperhead Press cartoon), the 1874 "Third Term Panic" cartoon, and early elephant appearances, including the 1876 "Political Situation" and the Rutherford B. Hayes tombstone cartoon. They also discuss the Wizard of Oz as a gold/silver allegory, Nast's decline when Harper's moved to photomechanical reproduction, and his death in Ecuador. The episode opens with banter about Georgia Sunday liquor sales and animal facts about donkeys, mules, hinnies and elephants. It closes with listener mail about a bison encounter in Alberta and a follow-up on the terms Indian versus Native American.
topics: Wizard of Oz gold standard allegory

segments.title: Opening banter and animal facts
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Georgia's Sunday alcohol sales vote, then discuss donkeys, mules, hinnies, and the donkey's reputation for self-preservation rather than stubbornness. They also cover matriarchal elephant herds and elephant mourning behavior.

segments.title: Thomas Nast and Uncle Sam
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Thomas Nast, a German-born cartoonist and woodblock carver who rose to fame in New York. They say he popularized Uncle Sam imagery, possibly inspired by meat packer Samuel Wilson.

segments.title: Nast and the modern Santa Claus
segments.summary: The hosts credit Nast with associating St. Nick with gift giving and adding elves in Harper's Weekly, and with making Santa fat and jolly by 1881.

segments.title: Nast's career at Harper's Weekly and early Republicans
segments.summary: Nast worked at Harper's Weekly from 1862 to 1886 and became a national celebrity. The hosts discuss how Republicans of his era were socially liberal and how party labels have shifted over time. Nast opposed inflationary policies such as free silver.

segments.title: First donkey cartoon and Third Term Panic
segments.summary: The 1870 cartoon showing a donkey labeled Copperhead Press kicking a dead lion is described as the donkey's first appearance. The 1874 Third Term Panic cartoon, which opposed a possible third term for Ulysses Grant, is also covered. Bayard grabbing a donkey by the tail is discussed.

segments.title: Elephant cartoons and the Hayes tombstone
segments.summary: The hosts describe the elephant's early uses, including 1864 and 1872, and the 1874 Stranger Things Have Happened cartoon with both animals. They cover the 1876 Political Situation cartoon and the Rutherford B. Hayes tombstone cartoon, and Nast's inclusive Thanksgiving image.

segments.title: Wizard of Oz allegory and the donkey's legacy
segments.summary: Frank Baum's Wizard of Oz is described as a political allegory, with the yellow brick road as the gold standard and silver shoes as free silver. The hosts note that Nast's symbols became part of the national fabric.
topics: Wizard of Oz gold standard allegory

segments.title: Nast's decline and death
segments.summary: Harper's moved to photomechanical reproduction, which exposed Nast's pen-and-ink weaknesses. He lost his income, tried his own paper, and was appointed to Ecuador by Teddy Roosevelt, where he died of yellow fever at age 62.

segments.title: Listener mail: bison and Indian terminology
segments.summary: A listener from Burlington, Ontario describes a bison encounter in Elk Island National Park. The hosts then respond to a listener about the terms Indian and Native American, citing a poll and asking for feedback.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The episode closes with a plug for the video podcast Stuff from the Future and an ad read.
